title: The Solar System and Stars
seo_title: Earth Sciences 11: The Solar System and Stars Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
short_title: the nebular hypothesis, stars and orbits
standard_text: Astronomy seeks to explain the origin and interactions of Earth and its solar system: the nebular hypothesis, the Sun, the life cycle of stars, Kepler's laws and orbits, and the Earth–Moon–Sun system. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Earth Sciences 11)
meta_desc: Free Earth Sciences 11 worksheets (BC Curriculum): the nebular hypothesis, stars and orbits. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The solar system formed from a spinning cloud of gas and dust.
body_html:
How to think about it

The nebular hypothesis: about 4.6 billion years ago a cloud of gas and dust collapsed under gravity; the centre became the Sun and the disk formed the planets. The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium.

Stars are born in nebulae, spend most of their lives on the main sequence, and end as white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes depending on their mass. Kepler's laws: orbits are ellipses, planets move faster near the Sun, and T² is proportional to a³.

Example

What powers the Sun?

Hydrogen → helium

Answer: nuclear fusion

Example

Where does a planet move fastest in its orbit?

Kepler's second law

Answer: closest to the Sun

Common mistakes

  • Thinking planets orbit in perfect circles.
  • Thinking the Sun burns like a fire.
  • Thinking all stars end as black holes.

faq.q: Why are the inner planets rocky?
faq.a: Near the young Sun it was too hot for ices, so only rock and metal condensed.

items.q: In a massive star, 3 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 3 × 2 = 6 protons → carbon.

items.q: In a star, 5 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 5 = 20; atomic number 2 × 5 = 10 (neon).

items.q: In the life of a Sun-like star, what comes right after the main-sequence star stage?

items.q: What is weight?
c: the force of gravity on an object
the amount of matter in an object
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on Jupiter is 25 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 5 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 5 × 25 = 125 N.

items.q: On Venus (g = 8.9 N/kg), Olivia's backpack weighs 400.5 N. What is its mass?
items.e: mass = weight ÷ g = 400.5 ÷ 8.9 = 45 kg.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on Jupiter is 25 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 60 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 60 × 25 = 1500 N.
